question: The First Carnatic War (1746-1748) came to an end with which treaty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748), also called the Treaty of Aachen, closed the First Carnatic War between the English and the French in India (प्रथम कर्नाटक युद्ध का अंत एक्स-ला-शापेल की संधि से हुआ)

 

• The Anglo-French rivalry in India was an extension of the European War of the Austrian Succession, so peace in Europe produced peace in the Carnatic as well.

 

• Under the settlement Madras, which the French had captured, was handed back to the English in exchange for French gains elsewhere.

 

• The three Carnatic Wars were fought between 1746 and 1763 for supremacy of power in south-eastern India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Second Carnatic War (1749-1754) ended with the Treaty of Pondicherry, and the Third (1758-1763) with the Treaty of Paris.

 

• The war was named 'Carnatic' because the main theatre was the Coromandel coast region ruled nominally by the Nawab of Arcot.

 

• Dupleix, Governor-General of French possessions in India, was the main French strategist in the first two wars.

 

• Aix-la-Chapelle is the French name for the German city of Aachen where the European treaty was signed.

 

NOTE

 

• Treaty of Pondicherry (Option 1): The Treaty of Pondicherry was the settlement of the Second Carnatic War in 1754-55, when both companies agreed to stay out of the internal affairs of Indian rulers, so it cannot be the closing treaty of the first war.

 

• Treaty of Paris (Option 2): The Treaty of Paris (1763) belongs to the Third Carnatic War and the Seven Years' War, establishing British supremacy over the French; it came fifteen years after the first war had finished.

 

• Treaty of Madras (Option 4): The Treaty of Madras was signed in 1769 to end the First Anglo-Mysore War between Hyder Ali and the English, so it is a Mysore treaty with no link to the Carnatic Wars.

question: Which pair of European rivals led their respective companies during the Second Carnatic War (1749-1754)?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Robert Clive and Dupleix.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the Second Carnatic War the English were represented by Robert Clive and the French by Dupleix (द्वितीय कर्नाटक युद्ध: क्लाइव बनाम डूप्ले)

 

• Both companies kept taking opposite sides in the succession disputes of Indian rulers, which is why a trade rivalry turned into a military contest.

 

• Clive's daring defence of Arcot is the best remembered episode of this war and made his reputation as a soldier.

 

• The war closed in 1754-55 with the Treaty of Pondicherry, by which the two companies agreed not to interfere in the internal affairs of Indian rulers.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dupleix was recalled to France in 1754 after the Company's directors judged his political ambitions too costly.

 

• Eyre Coote won the decisive Battle of Wandiwash in 1760 during the Third Carnatic War, while the French commander there was Count de Lally.

 

• Hector Munro commanded the English forces at Buxar in 1764, a battle fought in eastern India and not in the Carnatic.

 

• Warren Hastings became Governor of Bengal in 1772 and the first Governor-General in 1773, long after Dupleix had left India.

 

NOTE

 

• Eyre Coote and Lally (Option 2): Eyre Coote and Lally were the opposing commanders in the Third Carnatic War, culminating at Wandiwash in 1760; they were not the leaders in the earlier Second Carnatic War of 1749-54.

 

• Hector Munro and Bussy (Option 3): Hector Munro led the British at the Battle of Buxar in 1764, and Bussy was a French general in the Deccan; they never faced each other as the chief leaders of the Second Carnatic War.

 

• Warren Hastings and Dupleix (Option 4): Warren Hastings entered Bengal politics only in the 1750s as a junior clerk and rose to prominence in the 1770s, so he could not have opposed Dupleix, who left India in 1754.

question: Where did the British defeat the French in 1760 under Sir Eyre Coote, effectively deciding the Third Carnatic War?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Wandiwash.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Battle of Wandiwash (1760) was won by the British under Sir Eyre Coote and decided the Third Carnatic War (वांडीवाश का युद्ध, 1760)

 

• The English victory was followed by the fall of Pondicherry in 1761, which passed into British control and ended serious French military power in India.

 

• The war ended with the Treaty of Paris (1763), which confirmed British supremacy over the French in the subcontinent.

 

• After the treaty the French retained only a few trading posts such as Pondicherry and Chandernagore, shorn of military importance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Wandiwash lies in present-day Tamil Nadu, in the region that was then part of the Carnatic.

 

• The French commander defeated at Wandiwash was Count de Lally, who was later recalled and executed in France.

 

• The Third Carnatic War (1758-1763) coincided with the Seven Years' War in Europe, which explains the global scale of the Anglo-French conflict.

 

• Plassey in Bengal had been won three years earlier in 1757, giving the British a strong financial base for the southern campaign.

 

NOTE

 

• Plassey (Option 1): Plassey (23 June 1757) was fought in Bengal against Siraj-ud-Daulah, who was backed by a small French contingent, and had nothing to do with the main Anglo-French duel in the Carnatic.

 

• Buxar (Option 2): Buxar (22 October 1764) was fought four years after the war ended, against Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II, so it is a Bengal-Awadh battle and not a French defeat.

 

• Sobraon (Option 3): Sobraon (1846) was the decisive English victory in the First Anglo-Sikh War in Punjab, nearly ninety years after Wandiwash, and no French forces were involved there.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Treaty of Pondicherry (1754-55).

1. It ended the Second Carnatic War.

2. The British and the French agreed not to interfere in the internal affairs of Indian rulers.

3. It established British supremacy over the French in India.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Treaty of Pondicherry (1754-55) brought the Second Carnatic War to a close (द्वितीय कर्नाटक युद्ध का अंत)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the two companies promised not to meddle in the internal affairs of Indian rulers and to return the territories they had captured.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the treaty restored a balance between the rivals, and British supremacy over the French came only after Wandiwash (1760) and the Treaty of Paris (1763).

 

• The settlement was largely a failure of Dupleix's policy, as the Company's directors in Paris preferred peace to expensive political adventures.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dupleix's policy of backing Indian claimants for a price was the model later copied by the British, notably in Bengal.

 

• The French negotiator who replaced Dupleix and concluded the treaty was Godeheu.

 

• The next round of fighting, the Third Carnatic War, began in 1758 and ended with the Treaty of Paris (1763).

 

• The Carnatic Wars ended in a British victory because British naval power cut French supply lines to India.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): Here the combination 2 and 3 only fails because statement 3 is wrong: the 1754-55 treaty was an even-handed settlement, and British primacy over France was established later through the Treaty of Paris of 1763.

 

• 1 only (Option 3): 1 only is incomplete because statement 2 is also true; the main clause of the treaty was that neither company would intervene in the quarrels of Indian princes and captured places were returned.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): This selection of 1, 2 and 3 wrongly includes statement 3; the supremacy of the British over the French is the result of the Third Carnatic War and the Treaty of Paris, not of the Pondicherry settlement.

question:
Assertion (A): After the Third Carnatic War the French ceased to be a serious political rival of the British in India.

Reason (R): The British won decisively at Wandiwash in 1760 and took Pondicherry in 1761.

Choose the correct option.
option_1: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion: the defeat at Wandiwash (1760) and the loss of Pondicherry (1761) broke French power (फ्रांसीसी शक्ति का पतन)

 

• The Treaty of Paris (1763) then confirmed British supremacy over the French in the subcontinent, leaving France with a few unfortified trading posts.

 

• The French could still trade from Pondicherry, Chandernagore, Mahe, Karaikal and Yanam but could no longer raise armies or compete for political control.

 

• With France sidelined, the English East India Company was free to turn against Indian powers such as Mysore, the Marathas and Awadh.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Eyre Coote commanded the British side at Wandiwash and Count de Lally the French side.

 

• The Third Carnatic War (1758-1763) was the Indian theatre of the global Seven Years' War.

 

• Pondicherry, the French capital in India, had been rebuilt by Dupleix and was therefore a heavy loss in 1761.

 

• The earlier British victory at Plassey (1757) had given the Company the Bengal revenues needed to finance the southern war.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 2): The pairing is not merely two unrelated truths: the military collapse at Wandiwash and Pondicherry is exactly why France stopped being a rival, so R does explain A and this option understates the link.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): Assertion A is accurate, because France never again challenged the British for power in India after 1763, and R is also accurate, so declaring either of them false misreads the history of the war.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): Reason R is historically correct, since Coote's victory at Wandiwash and the fall of Pondicherry in 1761 are standard facts, so it cannot be dismissed as false while A is treated as true or false.

question: The Shahi Farman of 1717, often called the 'Magna Carta' of the East India Company, was issued by which Mughal emperor?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Farrukh Siyar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Shahi Farman granting trading privileges in Bengal was issued by Mughal emperor Farrukh Siyar in 1717 and is called the Magna Carta of the Company (कंपनी का मैग्ना कार्टा — फर्रुखसियर का फरमान)

 

• The decree gave the Company freedom of trade in Bengal, as the emperor was receiving little revenue from the province and hoped that at least something would come from the English.

 

• It was a valuable concession because it exempted Company goods from customs duties in exchange for a small annual payment.

 

• Later Nawabs of Bengal complained that the Company and its servants misused the exemption, a quarrel that led towards Plassey.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Earlier, around 1651, Shah Shuja had allowed the English free trade across Bengal, Bihar and Odisha for 3000 rupees a year.

 

• Farrukh Siyar also ordered the execution of Banda Bahadur, the Sikh leader, in 1716.

 

• Surman's embassy to the court of Farrukh Siyar in 1715-17 obtained the farman.

 

• Murshid Quli Khan was the Nawab who resented the privileges and tried to restrict the dastak misuse.

 

NOTE

 

• Bahadur Shah I (Option 1): Bahadur Shah I reigned from 1707 to 1712, before the Surman embassy, and he did not issue the trade decree of 1717; his rule was marked by the succession wars after Aurangzeb's death.

 

• Muhammad Shah (Option 2): Muhammad Shah ruled from 1719 to 1748 and is remembered for Nadir Shah's invasion of 1739, not for the Company's famous trade charter, which had already been granted by his predecessor.

 

• Shah Alam II (Option 3): Shah Alam II was the emperor of the Treaty of Allahabad, who granted the Diwani in 1765; that grant is separate from the farman of 1717 which gave the Company only commercial privileges.

question: Who was appointed Diwan of Bengal by Aurangzeb in 1700 and later became its first independent Nawab?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Murshid Quli Khan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Murshid Quli Khan was made Diwan of Bengal by Aurangzeb in 1700 and after 1707 became virtually independent, receiving the Nawabi in 1717 (मुर्शिद कुली खान — बंगाल का प्रथम स्वतंत्र नवाब)

 

• After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 he assumed complete control of Bengal while still sending a share of the revenue to Delhi.

 

• He ruled until 1727, and his son-in-law Shuja-ud-Din succeeded him as Nawab.

 

• His long, strong rule gave Bengal stability and the wealth that later attracted the Company's ambitions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Murshid Quli Khan shifted the capital of Bengal from Dhaka to Murshidabad, which was named after him.

 

• Bengal, Bihar and Odisha were administered together as the Nawabi of Bengal during this period.

 

• The year 1717 saw both his elevation as Nawab and the farman of Farrukh Siyar to the English.

 

• Alivardi Khan came later and seized power by defeating Sarfaraz Khan at Giria in 1740.

 

NOTE

 

• Shuja-ud-Din (Option 2): Shuja-ud-Din was the son-in-law who became Nawab after 1727; he did not hold the post of Diwan under Aurangzeb and was initially governor of Odisha rather than the founder of Bengal's autonomy.

 

• Alivardi Khan (Option 3): Alivardi Khan rose in Bihar and became Nawab in 1740 after killing Sarfaraz Khan, so he was not Aurangzeb's appointee of 1700 and not the first independent ruler of the province.

 

• Mir Jafar (Option 4): Mir Jafar was installed by Robert Clive after Plassey in 1757, more than fifty years after the events described, and his rise depended on British support and not on the Mughal emperor.

question:
Arrange the following Nawabs of Bengal in chronological order of their rule.

1. Sarfaraz Khan

2. Murshid Quli Khan

3. Alivardi Khan

4. Shuja-ud-Din
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2, 4, 1, 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is Murshid Quli Khan (1717-1727), Shuja-ud-Din (1727-1739), Sarfaraz Khan (1739-1740) and Alivardi Khan (1740-1756) (बंगाल के नवाबों का क्रम)

 

• Murshid Quli Khan was the first Nawab and his son-in-law Shuja-ud-Din followed him.

 

• Sarfaraz Khan, the son of Shuja-ud-Din, held power only briefly before Alivardi Khan defeated him in the Battle of Giria in 1740.

 

• Alivardi Khan then ruled for sixteen years and named his daughter's son Siraj-ud-Daulah as heir.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shuja-ud-Din, while Nawab, transferred control of Bihar to Alivardi Khan, who had served there.

 

• Alivardi Khan reportedly sent a large sum of money, about two crore rupees, to the Mughal emperor to legitimise his seizure of power.

 

• Siraj-ud-Daulah, the grandson of Alivardi, was the last independent Nawab of Bengal.

 

• Mir Jafar, Mir Qasim and later Nawabs ruled as dependents of the English Company.

 

NOTE

 

• 2, 1, 4, 3 (Option 1): The order 2, 1, 4, 3 puts Sarfaraz Khan before his father Shuja-ud-Din, which is impossible since Sarfaraz succeeded Shuja-ud-Din in 1739 and was removed by Alivardi in 1740.

 

• 4, 2, 1, 3 (Option 3): The order 4, 2, 1, 3 starts with Shuja-ud-Din, who in fact took over in 1727 after Murshid Quli Khan, the founder of the line, had died; Murshid Quli Khan therefore comes first.

 

• 2, 4, 3, 1 (Option 4): The order 2, 4, 3, 1 places Alivardi Khan before Sarfaraz Khan, but Alivardi became Nawab only by defeating and killing Sarfaraz at Giria in 1740, so Sarfaraz precedes him.

question: In 1740 Alivardi Khan overthrew Sarfaraz Khan in which battle?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Battle of Giria.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Alivardi Khan defeated Nawab Sarfaraz Khan in the Battle of Giria (1740) and himself became Nawab of Bengal (गिरिया का युद्ध, 1740)

 

• Alivardi had earlier been in charge of Bihar, which Shuja-ud-Din had handed over to him when he became Nawab.

 

• After winning the throne he offered a bribe of two crore rupees to the Mughal emperor to legitimise his past actions.

 

• He ruled from 1740 until 1756 and designated Siraj-ud-Daulah, the son of his youngest daughter, as his successor.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Giria is located in Murshidabad district, close to the Bhagirathi river.

 

• Alivardi Khan also fought the Maratha raids of Raghuji Bhonsle, which devastated western Bengal in the 1740s.

 

• A tribute payment of chauth to the Marathas was fixed by a treaty with Alivardi in 1751.

 

• Siraj became Nawab in April 1756 after Alivardi's death.

 

NOTE

 

• Battle of Plassey (Option 2): Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 between Siraj-ud-Daulah and Robert Clive, seventeen years after Giria, and its outcome made the British a political power in Bengal.

 

• Battle of Buxar (Option 3): Buxar took place on 22 October 1764 between the English under Munro and the allied forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II, which is unrelated to the succession struggle of 1740.

 

• Battle of Wandiwash (Option 4): Wandiwash (1760) was fought in the Carnatic between the British and the French; it was part of the Third Carnatic War and played no role in Bengal's Nawabi politics.

question: Who became the Nawab of Bengal after the death of Alivardi Khan in 1756?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Siraj-ud-Daulah.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Siraj-ud-Daulah, the son of Alivardi Khan's youngest daughter, became Nawab of Bengal in 1756 (सिराजुद्दौला — 1756-57)

 

• Alivardi had designated him as heir, although he faced rivals in his family such as his aunt Ghaseti Begum.

 

• His short reign lasted from 1756 to 1757 and ended with his defeat at Plassey.

 

• Siraj was the last independent Nawab of Bengal, since every Nawab after him depended on the English Company.

 

• His grandfather's sixteen-year rule from 1740 to 1756 ended with his death, which handed the young Nawab a throne already surrounded by court rivals and by English ambitions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Siraj's mother was the youngest daughter of Alivardi Khan, and he was brought up at Patna.

 

• In June 1756 he attacked Fort William in Calcutta after the English began fortifying it without his permission.

 

• The conspirators against him included Mir Jafar, Rai Durlabh, Jagat Seth and Ghaseti Begum.

 

• He was captured and killed after Plassey on the orders of Mir Jafar's son Miran.

 

NOTE

 

• Mir Jafar (Option 1): Mir Jafar was Alivardi's army commander and later Nawab only after Plassey in 1757, so he did not directly succeed Alivardi; he came to power through a British-backed conspiracy against Siraj.

 

• Mir Qasim (Option 2): Mir Qasim was Mir Jafar's son-in-law, installed by the English in 1760, four years after Alivardi's death, and not the immediate heir of the old Nawab.

 

• Murshid Quli Khan (Option 4): Murshid Quli Khan had died in 1727, long before Alivardi, and was the first Nawab of the line rather than the man who followed Alivardi Khan to the throne.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Black Hole Tragedy.

1. It took place after the Nawab attacked Fort William in Calcutta in June 1756.

2. The Nawab involved was Alivardi Khan.

3. According to the traditional account, 146 Britishers were confined and only 23 survived.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 3 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the English had begun fortifying Fort William without permission, and in June 1756 the Nawab attacked and captured it (ब्लैक होल त्रासदी, जून 1756)

 

• Statement 2 is incorrect: the Nawab was Siraj-ud-Daulah, who had succeeded Alivardi Khan only two months earlier.

 

• Statement 3 is correct as the traditional account: 146 British prisoners were put into a small room, and by the next day only 23 were alive.

 

• The incident, as described by Holwell, supplied Clive with the pretext for the reconquest of Calcutta, though historians doubt the numbers.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The fleeing British had taken refuge on Fulta Island, while others reached Madras.

 

• Robert Clive and Admiral Watson came from Madras and recaptured Calcutta in January 1757.

 

• By the Treaty of Alinagar the Nawab restored the Company's trading privileges after the recapture.

 

• The Nawab's governor of Calcutta, Manikchand, was bribed by Clive.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 2): Taken as an answer, 1 and 2 only is wrong because statement 3 is true as the traditional account and statement 2 is false; the Nawab at that time was Siraj-ud-Daulah, who attacked Calcutta in 1756.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): As a choice, 2 and 3 only falsely includes statement 2, which names Alivardi Khan, although Alivardi died in April 1756 and the attack on Fort William was ordered by his successor Siraj-ud-Daulah.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): The grouping 1, 2 and 3 treats all three as correct, but the Nawab was not Alivardi Khan; the tragedy occurred under Siraj-ud-Daulah, so statement 2 makes the whole combination incorrect.

question: On the bank of which river was the first English factory in Bengal established?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hugli.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first English factory in Bengal was established on the bank of the Hugli river (बंगाल में पहली अंग्रेज़ी फैक्ट्री हुगली नदी के किनारे)

 

• Around 1651 Shah Shuja permitted the English free trade in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha in return for 3000 rupees per year, and Hugli became their base.

 

• The English later moved to the villages of Sutanuti, Gobindpur and Kalikata, and Calcutta (Kolkata) was founded in 1698.

 

• The Hugli is a distributary of the Ganga, giving Bengal an outlet for river-borne and sea trade.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Shahi Farman of 1717 later widened their privileges in the province.

 

• Fort William was built in Calcutta, which grew into the capital of British India until 1911.

 

• The English first built a factory in India at Surat (1613), on the western coast.

 

• Fort St George at Madras (1639) was the earliest fortified English settlement on the Coromandel coast.

 

NOTE

 

• Ganga (Option 1): The Ganga is the main river, but the English factory was set up on its distributary, the Hugli, so naming the Ganga does not match the standard textbook statement of the place.

 

• Kaveri (Option 2): The Kaveri flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu in south India, far from Bengal, and no Bengal factory could have been on it; it belongs to the Mysore and Carnatic theatre.

 

• Mahanadi (Option 3): The Mahanadi is the main river of Odisha, and although the English did enter Orissa, the first Bengal factory was at Hugli and not on this river.

question: The Battle of Plassey was fought on
solution_text:
The correct answer is 23 June 1757.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 in Nadia district of West Bengal between Siraj-ud-Daulah and Robert Clive (प्लासी का युद्ध, 23 जून 1757)

 

• Siraj-ud-Daulah, with roughly 50,000 soldiers and a small French contingent, was defeated because Mir Jafar did not bring his army into the fight.

 

• It is considered one of the shortest battles in Indian history, lasting about one and a half hours, and was won more by conspiracy than by combat.

 

• The victory marked the foundation of British rule in India and was the Company's first major political-military triumph in the subcontinent.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Plassey (Palashi) lies on the Bhagirathi river, about 150 km north of Calcutta.

 

• Clive's force was small, with around 3,000 men, against the Nawab's much larger army.

 

• After the battle Mir Jafar paid the English a huge sum and was installed as Nawab.

 

• The great fortune obtained from Bengal after Plassey became a source of funds for the Company's later wars.

 

NOTE

 

• 20 June 1756 (Option 2): 20 June 1756 is the date on which Siraj-ud-Daulah captured Fort William in Calcutta and the Black Hole incident occurred, a year before Plassey, so it is the prelude and not the battle date.

 

• 22 October 1764 (Option 3): 22 October 1764 is the date of the Battle of Buxar, where the English under Hector Munro defeated Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II, which consolidated the earlier victory.

 

• 12 August 1765 (Option 4): 12 August 1765 is associated with the Treaty of Allahabad, by which the Mughal emperor granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company, a diplomatic settlement and not a battle.

question: Who among the following commanders of Siraj-ud-Daulah betrayed him by not bringing his army into the field at Plassey?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mir Jafar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mir Jafar, the Commander-in-Chief of the Nawab's army, kept his troops out of the fight at Plassey and so decided the day for Clive (मीर जाफर की गद्दारी)

 

• Clive had secretly set up Mir Jafar as Commander-in-Chief and made him the future Nawab in return for support.

 

• For this betrayal Mir Jafar was installed as Nawab of Bengal in 1757, and he paid the British a large sum, about one crore rupees.

 

• Other conspirators were Rai Durlabh the Dewan (revenue minister), the banker Jagat Seth and Siraj's aunt Ghaseti Begum.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mir Jafar was removed in 1760 because he could not supply enough money to the Company, and was restored in 1763.

 

• He died in 1765, and the English installed his son Najm-ud-Daula.

 

• The conspiracy had been drawn up with the help of William Watts and the merchant Omichand.

 

• Siraj-ud-Daulah fled the field and was later captured and executed.

 

NOTE

 

• Mir Madan (Option 1): Mir Madan was one of the few loyal officers who fought and was killed at Plassey, so he did not betray the Nawab and indeed his death was one of the setbacks for Siraj.

 

• Mohan Lal (Option 3): Mohan Lal was a loyal officer of the Nawab who fought bravely against Clive's army at Plassey and did not take part in the conspiracy, so he was not the man who held back.

 

• Manikchand (Option 4): Manikchand was the Nawab's governor of Calcutta, bribed by Clive in early 1757 to hand over the city, an earlier event than Plassey and unrelated to command of the field army.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Battle of Plassey.

1. It was fought in Nadia district of West Bengal.

2. Robert Clive commanded the British forces.

3. It is regarded as a long and bloody campaign of several months.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Plassey is in Nadia district, West Bengal, on the Bhagirathi river (नदिया ज़िला, प. बंगाल)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the British side was led by Robert Clive, who faced Siraj-ud-Daulah and a small French contingent.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the battle was one of the shortest in Indian history, lasting only about one and a half hours.

 

• The result was said to be won without a real fight, since the commanders on the Nawab's side had been won over by Clive.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• After the battle Clive had Mir Jafar proclaimed Nawab, and the British received the Zamindari of the 24 Parganas.

 

• The treasure of Murshidabad was transferred to Calcutta.

 

• Plassey raised the Company from a trading body to a territorial power, though the consolidation came with Buxar.

 

• The French contingent with Siraj was led by Sinfray, and Chandernagore had been taken by Clive shortly before.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): Such a pairing, 2 and 3 only is incorrect because it leaves out the true statement about location and adds a false claim; Plassey was over in about ninety minutes and not drawn out for months.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): In this form, 1 and 3 only drops Clive's command, which is a fact, and keeps the idea of a lengthy campaign, which is wrong because the encounter was a short, nearly bloodless affair settled by treachery.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Here the combination 1, 2 and 3 wrongly accepts the claim that the engagement was long and fierce; textbooks describe it as a brief battle whose outcome had been fixed in advance by the conspirators.

question:
Match the following people with their role in the conspiracy against Siraj-ud-Daulah.

Column A: (a) Mir Jafar (b) Rai Durlabh (c) Jagat Seth (d) Manikchand

Column B: (i) Banker (ii) Commander-in-Chief of the Nawab's army (iii) Dewan or revenue minister (iv) Governor of Calcutta
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mir Jafar was the Commander-in-Chief, Rai Durlabh the Dewan (revenue minister), Jagat Seth the banker and Manikchand the Nawab's governor of Calcutta (षड्यंत्रकारियों की भूमिका)

 

• Clive set up Mir Jafar as the head of the Nawab's army, which made his non-participation at Plassey decisive.

 

• Jagat Seth, the powerful banking magnate of Murshidabad, financed and supported the English cause.

 

• Manikchand was bribed by Clive, which enabled the attack on Calcutta and the treaty (Alinagar) forced on Siraj.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Siraj's aunt Ghaseti Begum also joined the group of the Nawab's opponents.

 

• The Treaty of Alinagar of February 1757 restored the English privileges after Calcutta's recapture.

 

• Clive then attacked the French colony at Chandernagore in 1757, which angered the Nawab.

 

• The Seths were bankers to the Nawabs of Bengal and handled the revenue remittances.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (Option 1): a-iii, b-ii swaps the roles of Mir Jafar and Rai Durlabh; Mir Jafar commanded the army while Rai Durlabh handled revenue as Dewan, so this pairing reverses two correct matches.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv (Option 2): a-ii, b-i, c-iii mixes up the banker and the revenue minister; Jagat Seth was the banker and Rai Durlabh the Dewan, which makes the second and third pairs wrong in this combination.

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i (Option 4): c-iv, d-i gives Jagat Seth the governorship and Manikchand the banking role, which is reversed; Manikchand governed Calcutta for Siraj, while Jagat Seth was the great banker.

question: Mir Qasim, installed as Nawab of Bengal in 1760, shifted his capital to
solution_text:
The correct answer is Munger.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mir Qasim moved his capital from Murshidabad to Munger (Monghyr) in Bihar, away from the influence of the Calcutta Council (मीर कासिम ने राजधानी मुंगेर स्थानांतरित की)

 

• He became Nawab after Mir Jafar was removed for failing to provide sufficient funds to the English.

 

• Possessing strong patriotic sentiments, he tried to build an independent army and reform the finances, which brought him into conflict with the Company.

 

• He was therefore removed and Mir Jafar was re-appointed, after which Mir Qasim took refuge in Awadh.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mir Qasim was the son-in-law of Mir Jafar.

 

• He ceded Burdwan, Midnapore and Chittagong to the Company in 1760.

 

• At Munger he set up a gun factory and trained a modern army.

 

• The abolition of internal transit duties, which hurt Company servants' private trade, led to the final break.

 

NOTE

 

• Murshidabad (Option 2): Murshidabad was the old capital from which Murshid Quli Khan and later Nawabs ruled, and Mir Qasim wanted to leave it so as to escape English pressure, so it is the place he left.

 

• Patna (Option 3): Patna was the base of Siraj's early years and an important Bihar city, but Mir Qasim chose Munger as his new seat; Patna was the scene of the 1763 clash with the English.

 

• Dhaka (Option 4): Dhaka had been the capital before Murshid Quli Khan moved it to Murshidabad in the early eighteenth century, so it was no longer the capital in 1760 and not Mir Qasim's choice.

question: Which of the following was NOT a member of the alliance that fought the English at the Battle of Buxar (1764)?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mir Jafar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mir Jafar was not in the anti-British alliance; he was the English-backed Nawab who had replaced Mir Qasim (बक्सर में मीर जाफर शामिल नहीं था)

 

• The allied army consisted of Mir Qasim (deposed Nawab of Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daulah (Nawab of Awadh) and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II.

 

• Mir Qasim, after being removed, took refuge in Awadh and joined hands with the others against the Company.

 

• The British force at Buxar was commanded by Hector Munro, and it won on 22 October 1764.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The battle took place in the Shahabad district on the bank of the Ganga in present-day Bihar.

 

• Buxar is often described as a more decisive battle than Plassey because the Company beat the combined army of the Mughal emperor and a major provincial ruler.

 

• Shuja-ud-Daulah was later made to pay an indemnity of 50 lakh rupees by the Treaty of Allahabad.

 

• Mir Qasim himself fled and died in obscurity in 1777 near Delhi.

 

NOTE

 

• Mir Qasim (Option 1): Mir Qasim fought at Buxar against the Company, so he was a member of the alliance; having been removed for his independent policies he fled to Awadh and sought help there.

 

• Shuja-ud-Daulah (Option 2): Shuja-ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Awadh, supplied the largest part of the allied troops and was a leading commander in the battle, so he was clearly on the side opposed to the English.

 

• Shah Alam II (Option 4): Shah Alam II, the Mughal emperor, was present with his troops on the allied side, and after defeat he agreed to the Treaty of Allahabad, so he cannot be the one outside the alliance.

question: The English victory at the Battle of Buxar is significant because
option_1: it gave the Company effective control over Bengal, Bihar and Odisha and a dominant position over Awadh and the Mughal Emperor
option_2: it ended the Company's trade monopoly in India
option_3: it made the French masters of Bengal
option_4: it led to the annexation of Punjab
solution_text:
The correct answer is it gave the Company effective control over Bengal, Bihar and Odisha and a dominant position over Awadh and the Mughal Emperor.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After Buxar (1764) the British gained effective control over Bengal, Bihar and Odisha and held a dominant position over Awadh and the Mughal Emperor (बक्सर के बाद ब्रिटिश प्रभुत्व)

 

• It is often said that the victory of Plassey was consolidated by the decisive victory at Buxar.

 

• The British had defeated not just a Nawab but an alliance including a sitting Mughal emperor and the ruler of Awadh.

 

• After the two battles the Company began establishing Residencies in Indian states and extended its influence towards southern Mysore.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Hector Munro was the British commander at Buxar, fought on 22 October 1764.

 

• The battle was followed in 1765 by the Treaty of Allahabad and the grant of the Diwani.

 

• Clive returned as Governor of Bengal in 1765 and began the dual system of government.

 

• Buxar showed that Indian armies, even large ones, were weaker than the Company's disciplined forces.

 

NOTE

 

• it ended the Company's trade monopoly in India (Option 2): The Company's trade monopoly was not ended by Buxar; on the contrary it was strengthened by the control of Bengal's revenue, and the monopoly was curtailed only by the Charter Act of 1813.

 

• it made the French masters of Bengal (Option 3): The French had been defeated in the Carnatic Wars and reduced to a few trading posts by 1763, so they were nowhere near becoming masters of Bengal after the battle of 1764.

 

• it led to the annexation of Punjab (Option 4): Punjab was annexed in 1849 after the Second Anglo-Sikh War, some eighty-five years after Buxar, and the 1764 victory in Bihar had no direct link with that annexation.

question: Under the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), which Mughal emperor granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the East India Company?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shah Alam II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• By the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II granted the Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the East India Company, with Robert Clive negotiating (इलाहाबाद की संधि, 1765)

 

• Diwani meant the right to collect revenue and to control civil justice, giving the Company enormous financial power.

 

• The same year Clive was appointed Governor of Bengal, and British power in India was thoroughly established.

 

• Clive then began the system of dual government, under which the Company had the Diwani and the Nawab retained the Nizamat.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The treaty was concluded after the defeat at Buxar and gave Shah Alam II the districts of Kora and Allahabad and a yearly payment.

 

• Awadh was restored to Shuja-ud-Daulah on payment of an indemnity.

 

• Dual government ended in 1772 when Warren Hastings took over the collection of revenue directly.

 

• Farrukh Siyar was the emperor of the earlier 1717 trade farman.

 

NOTE

 

• Farrukh Siyar (Option 1): Farrukh Siyar issued the Shahi Farman of 1717, a grant of trading privileges, and died in 1719, forty-six years before the Diwani was conferred, so he cannot be the grantor.

 

• Bahadur Shah Zafar (Option 3): Bahadur Shah Zafar was the last Mughal emperor, crowned in 1837 and the symbolic leader of the 1857 revolt, long after the Diwani had been granted in 1765.

 

• Akbar II (Option 4): Akbar II reigned from 1806 to 1837 and was a pensioner of the Company, so he came much later than 1765 and could not have conferred the Diwani on it.

question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order.

1. Battle of Buxar

2. Black Hole Tragedy

3. Treaty of Allahabad

4. Battle of Plassey
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2, 4, 1, 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sequence is the Black Hole Tragedy (June 1756), the Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757), the Battle of Buxar (22 October 1764) and the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) (घटनाओं का कालक्रम)

 

• In June 1756 Siraj-ud-Daulah seized Fort William after the English fortified it without permission.

 

• Plassey followed a year later, making the English a political power in Bengal.

 

• Buxar consolidated that victory, and the treaty of 1765 gave the Company the Diwani and secured its legal position.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Treaty of Alinagar (February 1757) falls between the Black Hole incident and Plassey.

 

• Mir Jafar became Nawab after Plassey in 1757 and was replaced by Mir Qasim in 1760.

 

• Mir Qasim was removed in 1763 and the third phase of the war led up to Buxar.

 

• Robert Clive went back to England in 1760 and returned as Governor of Bengal in 1765.

 

NOTE

 

• 2, 1, 4, 3 (Option 1): The order 2, 1, 4, 3 puts Buxar before Plassey, but Plassey was fought in 1757 and Buxar in 1764, so the second battle cannot come ahead of the first.

 

• 4, 2, 1, 3 (Option 2): The order 4, 2, 1, 3 places Plassey before the Black Hole incident, which is wrong because the capture of Fort William in 1756 provoked Clive's expedition culminating at Plassey.

 

• 2, 4, 3, 1 (Option 4): The order 2, 4, 3, 1 sets the Treaty of Allahabad before Buxar, yet the treaty was imposed after the victory at Buxar and so must be the last event in the sequence.

question: Why was Mir Jafar removed from the Nawabship of Bengal in 1760 and replaced by Mir Qasim?
option_1: He refused to recognise the Mughal emperor
option_2: He had allied with the French at Pondicherry
option_3: He had attacked Fort William in Calcutta
option_4: He failed to provide sufficient funds to the English Company
solution_text:
The correct answer is He failed to provide sufficient funds to the English Company.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mir Jafar had agreed to pay large sums to the Company for making him Nawab, but he failed to provide sufficient funds, so the English replaced him with Mir Qasim (धन की कमी के कारण मीर जाफर को हटाया गया)

 

• He had paid one crore rupees to the British, who then appointed him Nawab of Bengal after Plassey in 1757.

 

• The removal followed Clive's return to England, after which the Calcutta Council felt free to change the Nawab.

 

• The episode shows how the Company turned the Nawabship into a business, selling it to the highest bidder.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mir Qasim, in turn, was removed in 1763 when he asserted independence, and Mir Jafar was re-appointed.

 

• Mir Qasim agreed to cede Burdwan, Midnapore and Chittagong to the Company on being made Nawab.

 

• Mir Jafar died in 1765, and the Company continued to install his descendants.

 

• Mir Jafar's betrayal at Plassey earned him the label of traitor in Indian memory.

 

NOTE

 

• He refused to recognise the Mughal emperor (Option 1): Mir Jafar was himself a dependent of the English and had no quarrel with the Mughal emperor; the emperor's recognition was not the issue between him and the Calcutta Council.

 

• He had allied with the French at Pondicherry (Option 2): The French had been eliminated from Bengal when Chandernagore fell in 1757, and the French base at Pondicherry was far away, so Mir Jafar's removal had no connection to French alliances.

 

• He had attacked Fort William in Calcutta (Option 3): The attack on Fort William in Calcutta (June 1756) was carried out by Siraj-ud-Daulah, Mir Jafar's predecessor, and that event was the cause of Siraj's downfall and not of Mir Jafar's.

question: The system of 'Dual Government' in Bengal, in which the Company controlled revenue while administration stayed with the Nawab, was started by
solution_text:
The correct answer is Robert Clive.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Robert Clive started the Dual government in Bengal after the Company obtained the Diwani in 1765 (क्लाइव की द्वैध शासन प्रणाली, 1765)

 

• Clive was appointed Governor of Bengal in 1765, the same year as the Treaty of Allahabad conferred the Diwani on the Company.

 

• Under the arrangement the Company held the revenue powers while the Nawab held the Nizamat or criminal justice and policing.

 

• It gave the Company power without responsibility and had harmful effects on the people of Bengal.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Indian deputies administered the two functions, with Muhammad Reza Khan in Bengal and Raja Shitab Roy in Bihar.

 

• The system lasted until 1772, when Warren Hastings abolished it.

 

• The terrible famine of 1770 in Bengal occurred under this system.

 

• The Diwani brought Bengal's revenues directly to the Company, financing its further wars.

 

NOTE

 

• Warren Hastings (Option 1): Warren Hastings abolished dual government in 1772 and took over the collection of revenue directly, becoming the first Governor-General in 1773; he ended the arrangement rather than starting it.

 

• Lord Cornwallis (Option 3): Lord Cornwallis, who served as Governor-General from 1786 to 1793, is remembered for the Permanent Settlement and administrative reforms and for fighting Tipu, not for starting dual government.

 

• Lord Wellesley (Option 4): Lord Wellesley arrived as Governor-General in 1798 and is known for the Subsidiary Alliance and the Fourth Mysore War, many years after the Bengal dual system had been established.

question: Hyder Ali, who later became the ruler of Mysore, began his career as a petty army officer and was made head of the army at
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dindigul.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Hyder Ali rose from a petty officer in the Mysore army and, on account of his bravery, was appointed head of the army at Dindigul, where he trained his troops in European style (हैदर अली — डिंडीगुल में सेना प्रमुख)

 

• He ruled Mysore from 1761 to 1782 and made the state a formidable power in the south.

 

• He had to face revolts by Polygars, the warrior chieftains and local zamindars.

 

• The Marathas, the British and the Nizam of Hyderabad all planned to attack him, so he made a treaty with the Marathas, offering them 32 lakh rupees.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Nizam eventually withdrew support from the anti-Hyder alliance.

 

• Dindigul is in present-day Tamil Nadu and was an important fort.

 

• With French assistance Hyder built an arsenal at Dindigul for modern weapons.

 

• He is credited with using rockets in warfare, a technique that Tipu extended.

 

• His son Tipu inherited both his army and his dislike of the English.

 

NOTE

 

• Srirangapatna (Option 1): Srirangapatna was the capital of Mysore and the place where Tipu fell in 1799; it is not the place where Hyder's early army command is recorded in the textbook account.

 

• Bangalore (Option 2): Bangalore was a major Mysore fortress taken by Cornwallis in 1791 during the Third Anglo-Mysore War, and is not described as the training base of Hyder's troops.

 

• Arcot (Option 3): Arcot was the seat of the Nawab of the Carnatic, whom the English supported, and it belonged to the Carnatic region, not to the Mysore army command that Hyder Ali held in his early career.

question: The First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-1769) ended with the
solution_text:
The correct answer is Treaty of Madras.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The First Anglo-Mysore War between Hyder Ali and the British ended in the Treaty of Madras (1769), with Hyder Ali the victor (प्रथम आंग्ल-मैसूर युद्ध — मद्रास की संधि)

 

• Under the treaty the conquered territories were to be returned to each other.

 

• The two sides also promised mutual help in case either was attacked by a foreign power.

 

• The promise of help did not stop the quarrel; the British failed to assist Hyder against the Marathas in 1771, leading to the second war.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Hyder Ali had brought his army right up to the gates of Madras to force the treaty.

 

• The British had formed an alliance with the Nizam and the Marathas against Hyder at the start of the war.

 

• The war was fought during the Governor-Generalship period before Warren Hastings, in the age of the Madras Council.

 

• The treaty shows that in 1769 the Company could still be dictated terms to by an Indian ruler.

 

NOTE

 

• Treaty of Mangalore (Option 1): The Treaty of Mangalore was signed in 1784 at the end of the Second Anglo-Mysore War between Tipu Sultan and the English Company, a different conflict from that of 1767-69.

 

• Treaty of Srirangapattinam (Option 2): The Treaty of Srirangapattinam (1792) closed the Third Anglo-Mysore War, after which Tipu Sultan had to surrender half of his territories, so it belongs to a later struggle.

 

• Treaty of Bassein (Option 4): The Treaty of Bassein (1802) was concluded between the Peshwa Baji Rao II and the British under Wellesley, a Maratha treaty that is not part of the Mysore wars.
